title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two fragments from Euler's notebooks, both attributed to J. A. Euler.

§109 is an arcsine integral produced by a Möbius substitution. Put y = (bp+aq)/(ap+bq), where p and q are any functions of one variable. Then:
- 1−y² = (a²−b²)(p²−q²)/(ap+bq)²;
- dy = (a²−b²)(p dq − q dp)/(ap+bq)².
Hence ∫ (p dq − q dp)√(a²−b²) / [(ap+bq)√(p²−q²)] = arcsin[(bp+aq)/(ap+bq)].
Two specialisations follow:
- (I) p=1, q=x gives ∫ dx√(a²−b²)/[(a+bx)√(1−x²)] = arcsin[(b+ax)/(a+bx)]. This is the standard reduction of ∫dx/((a+bx)√(1−x²)).
- (II) p=1+x², q=x√2. Then p dq − q dp = √2(1−x²)dx and p²−q² = 1+x⁴. This gives an elementary (arcsine) evaluation of ∫ √2√(a²−b²)(1−x²)dx / [(a(1+x²)+bx√2)√(1+x⁴)]. That is a pseudo-elliptic integral: the radical √(1+x⁴) is quartic, yet the integral is elementary. The mechanism is that 1+x⁴ is written as a difference of squares of quadratics.

§110, 'Specimen methodi facilis Analysin infinitorum indeterminatam tractandi', asks for algebraic rectifiable plane curves.
- Set dx = ds cosφ, dy = ds sinφ.
- Make the ansatz x = s cosφ + p, y = s sinφ + q. Requiring dx = ds cosφ and dy = ds sinφ forces dp = s sinφ dφ and dq = −s cosφ dφ.
- Hence tanφ = −dp/dq and s = dp/(sinφ dφ) = −dp/d(cosφ).
- Choose any algebraic relation between p and q. Then φ (through its sine and cosine), s, x and y are all algebraic, so (x,y) is an algebraic rectifiable curve.

Geometrically, (cosφ, sinφ) is the unit normal of the auxiliary curve (p,q), and s is its radius of curvature. So (x,y) = (p,q) + s·n is the evolute of an arbitrary algebraic curve, and (p,q) is an involute of (x,y). The arc length is the difference of curvature radii. This is Huygens' observation that evolutes of algebraic curves are algebraically rectifiable, here dressed as a 'method of indeterminate analysis'.

The page then starts §5, attributed to Lexell, on algebraic curves whose rectification depends on a prescribed quadrature. It continues on the next page, leading to Euler's problem of rectifiable curves on the sphere, dx² sin²y + dy² = dr².
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. §109 checks out: 1−y² = (a²−b²)(p²−q²)/(ap+bq)², dy = (a²−b²)(pdq−qdp)/(ap+bq)², and in II p dq − q dp = √2(1−x²)dx, p²−q² = 1+x⁴.
In II the constant should read √2·√(a²−b²). The print 'dx(1−xx)√2(aa−bb)' is ambiguous; if the radical is read over 2(aa−bb), the coefficient comes out as √(2(a²−b²)), which is wrong.
§110.3: s = dp/(dφ sinφ) = −dp/d.cosφ is correct, since d cosφ = −sinφ dφ.
Integration constants are omitted throughout, which is harmless.
§110 does not mention degenerate cases (e.g. dφ = 0, where (p,q) is a straight line).

ideas.what: Arcsine integrals from the linear-fractional substitution y = (bp+aq)/(ap+bq), with the general identity ∫(pdq−qdp)√(a²−b²)/((ap+bq)√(p²−q²)) = arcsin y
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century integral calculus (Euler, Institutiones calculi integralis)
ideas.where_published: Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis vol. I treats such integrals; the exact general p,q form is unsure

ideas.what: Elementary (arcsine) evaluation of an integral containing √(1+x⁴), via p=1+x², q=x√2 so that p²−q² = 1+x⁴
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (several examples of this type in his integral calculus works); general theory Abel, Chebyshev, Zolotarev
ideas.where_published: Similar examples with √(1+x⁴) occur in Euler's integral-calculus papers; this exact two-parameter form is unsure

ideas.what: Algebraic rectifiable curves as x = s cosφ + p, y = s sinφ + q, with tanφ = −dp/dq and s = dp/(sinφ dφ), from an arbitrary algebraic relation between p and q
ideas.modern_name: Evolute of an algebraic curve (arc length = difference of radii of curvature); support-function/involute parametrization
ideas.usually_credited_to: Huygens (1673, evolutes); Leibniz, Johann Bernoulli; Euler's papers on algebraic rectifiable curves
ideas.where_published: Euler's memoirs on algebraic rectifiable curves (Opera omnia I.28); exact E-number unsure

ideas.what: Start of Lexell's variant: algebraic curves whose arc length reduces to a prescribed quadrature
ideas.modern_name: Curves with arc length given by a prescribed abelian integral / transcendental
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lexell (Acta Petropolitana papers on curves whose arcs are measured by given quadratures)
ideas.where_published: Likely related to published Euler/Lexell memoirs on rectification; unsure

deep.surprise_reason: Both fragments are textbook material for the period: a Möbius-substitution arcsine integral (with a mild pseudo-elliptic example) and Huygens' evolute construction of algebraic rectifiable curves, which Euler published in several memoirs. Nothing appears new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: In II the image's radical (√2 vs √(2(aa−bb))) is ambiguous; the mathematically correct factor is √2·√(aa−bb).
'\tang' should be rendered tang φ (tan φ).
§110.3 'd.cos φ' means the differential d(cos φ).
